title: Comprehension Skills
tagline: Comprehension · reading closely, answering precisely, inference and summary

sourceNote.boardprep: The practice passage, notes, model summary, vocabulary, questions and answers on this page are original BoardPrep material written for practice. All names and places in the passage are fictional, and nothing is taken from any textbook, guide or past paper.

overview.intro: A comprehension test asks you to read an unseen passage and show that you have understood what it says, what it suggests and how it is written. Good answers are not copied lines: they are short, accurate replies in your own words, backed by evidence from the passage. This chapter teaches a reading routine, the main question types, and a full practice passage with questions.

learn.title: A reading routine: skim, then read closely

blocks.text: Do not begin by reading every word slowly, and do not begin by hunting for answers. Move through the passage in two passes so that you understand the whole before you handle the details.

items: First pass (skim): read the title if there is one, the first sentence of each paragraph and the last paragraph. Ask yourself who, where and what is happening.
Second pass (close reading): read the whole passage steadily with a pencil. Underline names, dates, numbers, reasons and any sentence that seems important.
Glance at the questions before or after the second pass, as you prefer, so that you know what to look for.
Mark unfamiliar words but do not stop. Often the sentence around the word explains it.
Answer the questions in order. Return to the passage for every answer instead of trusting your memory.

learn.title: Finding evidence and answering in your own words

blocks.text: Every answer has an evidence sentence somewhere in the passage. Find it first, then decide how much of it the question needs. The best answers are complete sentences that use the words of the question and, where possible, your own vocabulary.

items.meaning: Match the key words in the question with the passage. Questions usually follow the order of the passage, so the answer to question 3 lies after the answer to question 2.
Take just the part of the evidence that answers the question. Copying a whole paragraph shows that you have not understood which part is relevant.
Change the wording where you can, without changing the meaning. Do not change key facts such as names, numbers or reasons.
Begin by turning the question into the start of your answer, so that the answer makes sense on its own.

items.text: Question: Why did the family leave early? Weak answer: 'Because of the rain.' Better answer: 'The family left early because heavy rain had begun and they feared the road would flood.'
items.note: The better answer is a full sentence and gives the reason, not just a word.

items.text: Question: What did the boy do first? Weak answer: copying three sentences from the passage. Better answer: 'The boy first tied his shoelaces and then ran to the gate.'
items.note: Take only the relevant event and put it in one clear sentence.

learn.title: Inference, vocabulary in context and tone

blocks.text: Some questions cannot be answered by finding one sentence. They ask what the passage suggests, what a word means in that place, or what mood the writer creates. These questions still need evidence, but you must think one step beyond the words.

items.meaning: A conclusion you reach from clues in the passage. State the conclusion and then name the clue that led to it. Example: if a character keeps checking the clock and bites her nails, you may infer that she is anxious.

The meaning a word has in this particular sentence. Read the words before and after it, try replacing it with your guess, and check that the sentence still makes sense. Use a word or phrase of the same part of speech.
The writer's attitude or the mood of the passage, such as humorous, hopeful, sorrowful, admiring, critical or matter-of-fact. Support your choice with two or three words or details from the text.
Questions such as 'What does it refer to?' ask which noun a pronoun stands for. Look at the nearest earlier noun that fits the sense.

blocks.text: Read the passage below with the routine you have just learnt, then attempt the questions in the practice set. Each question begins 'Refer to the practice passage'. The passage and all its names are fictional and written by BoardPrep.
The Library in the Grain Store

When Meenal Iyer returned to her grandfather's village of Karanpur after twelve years in the city, she first noticed the silence of the old grain store beside the temple. Its wooden doors had sagged, its windows were dull with dust, and pigeons nested in the rafters. Her grandfather said the store had once held the harvest of forty families, but since the new cooperative godown was built on the highway, nobody had needed it.

Meenal had an idea. She had brought two suitcases of books and could not bear to see them locked away again. She asked the village council for permission to use the grain store as a library. The council was doubtful. 'Who will read?' asked the headman, Mr. Deshmukh. 'Our people are busy with their fields.' Yet he agreed to let her try for three months, provided she did not ask for money.

In the first week, only Meenal and the pigeons visited. Then a boy named Tarun, who sold peanuts at the bus stop, wandered in to escape the afternoon heat and stayed until sunset with a picture book on rockets. The next day he returned with two friends. Within a month the children had painted the shelves blue, repaired the doors and made a rule that every borrowed book must be returned with a one-line opinion written on a slip of paper.

The adults followed slowly. Farmers came on rainy days, when the fields were too wet to work, and one grandmother, who had never learnt to read, asked the children to read aloud to her. By the end of the three months, the headman himself was seen carrying home a book about soil. He said nothing about the deadline. Instead, he quietly gave Meenal the key to the store, and the village council voted to pay for a lamp above the door so that the library could stay open after dark.

A summary keeps the main points of a passage and drops the rest. It should be written in your own words, in the third person and the past tense (unless the passage is about general truths), and it should be much shorter than the original. Follow the word limit given in the question.

items: Underline the main points while reading: who did what, why, and with what result.
Leave out examples, direct speech, repeated ideas and small descriptive details.
Join the points into connected sentences with linking words, not a list of fragments.
Do not add your own opinion or any fact that is not in the passage.
Count your words, then trim adjectives and repeated words if you are over the limit.

blocks.text: MODEL SUMMARY of the practice passage (about 60 words): Meenal Iyer, back in her grandfather's village after twelve years, asked to turn the unused grain store into a library. The headman allowed a three-month trial without funds. Children, starting with a peanut seller named Tarun, repaired and painted the place, and adults gradually joined them. Convinced, the headman gave her the key and the council paid for a lamp.

learn.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them

items: Copying long stretches of the passage. Pick only the part that answers the question and rephrase it where you can.
Answering in fragments such as 'Because of the heat'. Write a complete sentence that could be understood without the question.
Using outside knowledge. Every answer must be supported by the passage in front of you.
Guessing a word's meaning from the dictionary instead of from the sentence. A word can have several meanings.
Naming a tone without evidence. Always quote or mention two or three words that show it.
Writing a summary that is a shortened copy of the first paragraph. A summary must cover the whole passage.
Ignoring the number of marks or the word limit. Give as many points as the marks suggest and stay within the word limit in the question.

keyPoints: Skim first for the general idea, then read closely with a pencil.
Every answer needs an evidence sentence in the passage; go back and find it.
Answer in complete sentences and in your own words, lifting only what is relevant.
An inference is a conclusion supported by a clue; state both.
Vocabulary questions ask for the meaning in that sentence, so test your answer by substituting it.
Support the tone you name with words or details from the text.
A summary covers the whole passage, uses your own words and leaves out examples and speech.
examFocus: Locating the right part of the passage for each question.
Answering in complete, accurate sentences without copying long stretches.
Drawing inferences that are backed by a clue in the passage.
Working out the meaning of words and phrases from context.
Identifying the tone or attitude and supporting it with evidence.
Writing a concise summary within the word limit given in the question.

vocabulary.meaning: sank or bent downwards in the middle, usually from weight or age
vocabulary.context: The old shelf sagged under the weight of the encyclopaedias.

vocabulary.meaning: the sloping wooden beams that support a roof
vocabulary.context: A family of sparrows had built a nest in the rafters of the shed.

vocabulary.meaning: owned and run jointly by the people who use it
vocabulary.context: The farmers sold their milk through a cooperative society and shared the profit.

vocabulary.meaning: a group of people chosen to make decisions for a community
vocabulary.context: The school council met on Friday to plan the sports day.

vocabulary.meaning: not sure; feeling that something may not work
vocabulary.context: She was doubtful about crossing the swollen stream without a guide.

vocabulary.meaning: on the condition that; as long as
vocabulary.context: You may borrow my cycle, provided you return it before dark.

vocabulary.meaning: walked slowly without a fixed purpose or direction
vocabulary.context: The little girl wandered into the garden looking for her kitten.

vocabulary.meaning: the time or date by which something must be finished
vocabulary.context: The deadline for the project is the last day of the month.

questions.prompt: Refer to the practice passage. Why had the old grain store in Karanpur fallen out of use?
questions.answer: The grain store had fallen out of use because a new cooperative godown had been built on the highway, so nobody needed the old store any longer.
questions.explanation: Evidence: 'since the new cooperative godown was built on the highway, nobody had needed it.' One mark for the godown on the highway and one for the resulting lack of need.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that it was old and dusty. That describes its condition, not the reason it was abandoned.

questions.prompt: Refer to the practice passage. On what conditions did the headman allow Meenal to use the grain store?
questions.answer: The headman let Meenal try the library for three months, provided that she did not ask the village for money.
questions.explanation: Two conditions are needed: a trial period of three months and no request for money. The word 'provided' in the passage signals the condition.
questions.commonMistake: Mentioning only the three months and forgetting that she was not to ask for money.

questions.prompt: Refer to the practice passage. Why did Tarun first walk into the grain store?
options: He wanted to borrow a book about soil.
He wanted to escape the afternoon heat.
Meenal had invited him to paint the shelves.
He was looking for the headman.
questions.answer: He wanted to escape the afternoon heat.
questions.explanation: The passage says Tarun 'wandered in to escape the afternoon heat'. The book about soil was taken home later by the headman, and the shelves were painted after the children had begun to visit regularly.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the painting option because the children later painted the shelves.

questions.prompt: Refer to the practice passage. What rule did the children make about borrowed books?
options: Every book must be returned within three days.
Every borrower must pay a small fine for late return.
Every book must be returned with a one-line opinion on a slip of paper.
Every book must be read aloud to an elder.
questions.answer: Every book must be returned with a one-line opinion on a slip of paper.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states the rule exactly. The passage says nothing about fines or a time limit, and reading aloud is mentioned only in connection with the grandmother.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the option about reading aloud, which belongs to a different sentence in the passage.

questions.prompt: Refer to the practice passage. In the sentence 'he agreed to let her try for three months, provided she did not ask for money', the word 'provided' means
questions.explanation: Replace 'provided' with 'on the condition that' and the sentence keeps its meaning: he agreed, but only if she did not ask for money. 'Supplied' is a different meaning of the same word and does not fit here.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing 'supplied' because it is the meaning most often learnt for the word.

questions.prompt: Refer to the practice passage. Fill in the blank with one word taken from the first paragraph: The wooden doors of the store had ______, hanging low from their hinges.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says 'Its wooden doors had sagged', meaning they had sunk or bent downwards with age.
questions.commonMistake: Writing 'sagging', which does not fit the past perfect form had + past participle.

questions.prompt: Refer to the practice passage. Fill in the blank with a word from the second paragraph that means 'not sure': The council was ______ about turning the grain store into a library.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says 'The council was doubtful', and the headman's question 'Who will read?' shows the reason for the doubt.
questions.commonMistake: Using 'doubting' or 'doubt', which do not fit after 'was'.

questions.prompt: Refer to the practice passage. What can you infer about the headman's opinion of the library by the end of the three months? Give two clues from the passage.
questions.answer: By the end of the three months the headman had changed his mind and now valued the library. He was seen carrying home a book about soil, which shows that he had begun to use it himself, and he said nothing about the deadline but quietly gave Meenal the key to the store, which shows that he had decided to let it stay.
questions.explanation: One mark for the inference (his doubt had gone and he approved) and one mark for each clue: the soil book and the key given without mention of the deadline.
questions.commonMistake: Stating that he was pleased without naming a clue from the text.

questions.prompt: Refer to the practice passage. The grandmother 'had never learnt to read' but still visited the library. What does this suggest about the library and about the children?
questions.answer: It suggests that the library was welcoming even to people who could not read, because they could still enjoy books when someone read to them. It also shows that the children had become confident and helpful readers, since they were willing to read aloud to an elder in the village.
questions.explanation: One mark for the idea that the library served people beyond readers, one for the role of reading aloud, and one for what it shows about the children. Answers should stay close to the evidence: she asked the children to read aloud to her.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that the grandmother learnt to read at the library; the passage does not say this.

questions.prompt: Refer to the practice passage. Describe the overall tone of the passage in one or two words and support your choice with two pieces of evidence.
questions.answer: The tone is warm and hopeful. It begins with an empty, silent store but ends with a lamp being paid for so that the library can stay open after dark, which suggests growing life and hope. The gentle change in the doubtful headman, who quietly hands over the key, and the picture of children painting the shelves blue also create a warm, encouraging mood.
questions.explanation: One mark for a suitable tone word such as warm, hopeful, encouraging or gently admiring; two marks for evidence from the text; one mark for a clear explanation. A tone such as 'sad' or 'humorous' would not be supported by the passage.
questions.commonMistake: Naming the tone but giving no words or events from the passage as proof.

questions.prompt: Refer to the practice passage. Write a summary of the passage in about 60 words.
questions.answer: Meenal Iyer, back in her grandfather's village after twelve years, asked to turn the unused grain store into a library. The headman allowed a three-month trial without funds. Children, starting with a peanut seller named Tarun, repaired and painted the place, and adults gradually joined them. Convinced, the headman gave her the key and the council paid for a lamp.
questions.explanation: Marking checklist: the idea of an unused store turned into a library (1); the headman's doubt and the three-month trial (1); the children's work (1); adults joining (1); the headman's change of heart and the council's lamp (1); own words, connected sentences and close to the word limit (1).
questions.commonMistake: Copying the first paragraph and stopping there, or including the dialogue and the detail of the suitcases.

questions.prompt: Refer to the practice passage. What did the children do to the grain store within a month of Tarun's first visit?
questions.answer: Within a month the children painted the shelves blue, repaired the doors, and made a rule that each borrowed book must be returned with a one-line opinion on a slip of paper.
questions.explanation: One mark for each of the three actions: painting the shelves, repairing the doors and making the rule about opinion slips.
questions.commonMistake: Adding that the children paid for the lamp; that was done by the village council.
